# Early hominins · c. 2 million years ago

Around 2 million years ago: the first toolmakers and early Homo in Africa with Paranthropus beside them, Homo erectus across Eurasia with fire and handaxes, animals crossing the new Isthmus of Panama, and the ice ages beginning. Drag the timeline to move through time; click a dot to read that story here.

## origin-of-mankind
### Early Homo in Africa · 2.8 to 1.5 million years ago
spot: 3.5, 36
view: fit
site: Olduvai Gorge · -2.99, 35.35
site: Sterkfontein · -26.02, 27.73
area: East African Rift · -1, 36.5
area: Sahara · 23, 10

The oldest fossils placed in our genus come from **Ledi-Geraru** in Ethiopia, about 2.8 million years old, and flaked stone tools are at least 2.6 million years old. By 2 million years ago several kinds of early Homo lived around the **East African Rift**, in the caves of southern Africa and, on sparser evidence, farther north and west.

**Homo erectus** appears in East Africa by about 1.9 million years ago. The Nariokotome skeleton, 1.6 million years old, shows a tall, long-legged walker, and large handaxes follow from about 1.76 million years ago.

- early-homo: **Early Homo** · movement within Africa

> Every line runs outward: these are expansions, not exchange. Fossil sites date presence; the corridors between them are reconstructions and remain uncertain, and the West African branch rests on sparse evidence.

## homo-erectus
### Homo erectus across Eurasia · from 1.8 million years ago
spot: 41.7, 44.3
view: fit
site: Dmanisi · 41.7, 44.3
site: Sangiran · -7.4, 110.8
site: Atapuerca · 42.35, -3.5
site: Zhoukoudian · 39.7, 115.9
area: Wallacea · -5.5, 123

At **Dmanisi** in Georgia five skulls date to about 1.85–1.77 million years ago: small-brained people already far outside Africa. Stone tools at Shangchen in China may be 2.1 million years old; Homo erectus was on **Java** by about 1.3 million years ago, possibly earlier, and in Europe by about 1.4 million years ago, with Homo antecessor at Atapuerca and footprints at Happisburgh around 900,000 years ago.

Crossing sea gaps, hominins reached **Flores** by about a million years ago and **Luzon** by about 700,000 years ago, where small-bodied species later evolved. None of these dispersals is a direct line to living people.

- erectus: **Homo erectus & relatives** · repeated dispersals out of Africa

> Sites date presence; the corridors between them are reconstructions. Whether the first Eurasians were Homo erectus or an earlier form is debated.

[Sources and route notes ↗](./human-migrations-sources.md)

## first-tools
### The first toolmakers · 3.3 to 2.4 million years ago
spot: 11.1, 40.5
view: -8, 0 → 40, 48
site: Lomekwi · 3.95, 35.85
site: Gona · 11.1, 40.5
site: Ain Boucherit · 36.3, 5.4
area: Turkana Basin · 4, 36.4

The oldest known stone tools come from **Lomekwi**, west of Lake Turkana: cores and flakes about 3.3 million years old, made before our genus existed, perhaps by Kenyanthropus or an australopith. From about 2.6 million years ago the sharper, more regular **Oldowan** toolkit appears at **Gona** in the Afar and at Ledi-Geraru, where a jaw about 2.8 million years old is the oldest fossil placed in Homo.

By 2.4 million years ago Oldowan tools and cut-marked bones lie at **Ain Boucherit** in Algeria, at the other end of the continent: toolmaking was not confined to the Rift. Whether one lineage carried the idea or several invented it is an open question.

> No routes are drawn: tools do not travel on their own, and the makers of the oldest ones are unknown.

[Sources and route notes ↗](./human-migrations-sources.md)

## paranthropus
### The other hominins · 2.7 to 1 million years ago
spot: -2.3, 36
view: fit
site: Peninj · -2.3, 36
site: Koobi Fora · 3.95, 36.3
site: Swartkrans · -26, 27.7

Alongside early Homo lived a second line of hominins with huge cheek teeth and heavy jaws: **Paranthropus**. Its oldest form appears in the Turkana Basin about 2.7 million years ago; Paranthropus boisei, the "Nutcracker Man" found at Olduvai in 1959, ranged across East Africa until about 1.3 million years ago, and Paranthropus robustus lived in the caves of the **Cradle of Humankind**, at **Swartkrans** and Kromdraai, from about 2 million years ago.

Isotopes in their teeth show that boisei ate mostly grasses and sedges, a diet no living ape has. For a million years two kinds of upright hominin shared the same valleys; only one line went on.

- paranthropus: **Paranthropus** · range across eastern and southern Africa

> The line marks a range between fossil sites, not a journey. Paranthropus left no descendants.

[Sources and route notes ↗](./human-migrations-sources.md)

## fire-and-handaxes
### Fire and handaxes · 1.8 to 0.8 million years ago
spot: 5.3, 37.4
view: fit
site: Konso · 5.3, 37.4
site: Ubeidiya · 32.7, 35.55
site: Attirampakkam · 13.2, 80
site: Wonderwerk Cave · -27.85, 23.55
area: Levant · 34.5, 37

From about 1.76 million years ago hominins in East Africa began shaping stone on both faces into teardrop **handaxes** and cleavers, the Acheulean toolkit, first at **Konso** in Ethiopia and Kokiselei in Kenya. The design travelled with its makers: to **Ubeidiya** in the Jordan valley by about 1.5 million years ago, to **Attirampakkam** near Chennai at about the same time, west to Casablanca and south to the edge of the Kalahari, and it stayed in use for more than a million years.

Fire came into use in the same span. Reddened patches at Koobi Fora 1.5 million years ago are debated, but ash and burnt bone deep inside **Wonderwerk Cave** about a million years ago, and hearths at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel around 790,000 years ago, show fire being kept and used.

- handaxes: **Handaxes** · the Acheulean toolkit carried out of East Africa

> Arrows follow the order of dated sites; the makers' actual paths are unknown, and the Acheulean may have been invented more than once.

## american-interchange
### Beasts across Panama · from 2.7 million years ago
spot: 8.5, -80
view: fit
area: Isthmus of Panama · 9.5, -79
area: Pampas · -34, -62
area: Great Plains · 40, -100

While hominins spread across Africa, the two Americas met. Around 2.8 million years ago the **Isthmus of Panama** closed the seaway between the oceans, and animals that had evolved apart for tens of millions of years crossed in both directions: the **Great American Biotic Interchange**. Southbound went horses, camels (the ancestors of llamas), deer, dogs, bears, cats and gomphotheres, cousins of the elephants. Northbound went ground sloths, glyptodonts, armadillos, capybaras, porcupines and opossums, and the terror bird Titanis reached Florida.

The northern newcomers prospered and make up much of South America's mammals today; most of the southern natives that went north later died out. The closing also rerouted the currents that feed the Gulf Stream, one of the changes that set the ice ages going.

- north-bound: **Northbound** · South American animals into North America
- south-bound: **Southbound** · North American animals into South America

> The lines are schematic corridors across the land bridge, not the path of any one species. Dates for the closing of the isthmus range from about 10 to 3 million years ago; the main pulses of animals came after 2.7 million.

[Sources and route notes ↗](./human-migrations-sources.md)

## cooling-world
### A cooling world · from 2.6 million years ago
spot: 72, -40
view: 55, -80 → 85, 20
area: Greenland · 74, -42
area: Sahara · 23, 10

The Pleistocene begins 2.58 million years ago, when ice sheets that had been growing on **Greenland** spread across North America and Eurasia. From then on the climate swung between glacials and warm spells, every 41,000 years at first and every 100,000 years after about 900,000 years ago, with sea level falling and rising by more than a hundred metres each time.

The **Sahara** turned green and dry again with the monsoon, and the lakes of the East African Rift filled and vanished in the same rhythm; grassland spread at the expense of forest. Many of the changes in hominins, in Paranthropus and in the animals around them fall into these pulses. Elsewhere the giant shark Megalodon had just gone extinct, and Gigantopithecus, an ape three metres tall, lived in the forests of southern China.

> No routes: this story is the weather. Its dates come from ocean sediment and ice cores, not from sites on the map.
